body: At twenty to two the house is still up in pieces. Ma and his father are doing Santa in the front room in their church clothes, in whispers, bringing the boxes down from the hall closet two at a time, and Nonna sleeps in her chair through all of it with Theo’s throw over her knees and the tree lights left on for her. His father carried Rosie up from the truck asleep, and Gina has gone to bed. With the incense from St. Brigid’s still in the wool of his good coat, Jack goes down the basement stairs in his socks to shut off the Dell for Gina, and doesn’t. The laundry sink is empty for the first time since Monday, scrubbed, the plate and the can of Contadina put away; the baccalà went to the table six hours ago and didn’t come back. The screen saver is drifting blue over the paneling. He moves the mouse, and at the top of the page it says *Inbox (1)*.

body.name: Lena Broussard
body.text: Merry Christmas from the pew behind the one Grandmère sat in. Remy is asleep sitting up. Mama has already been to the church once today and come back. Pray for me at yours and I’ll pray for you at mine, an hour late, the way we do everything. —L.

body: Down there it’s twenty to one. They’ll be about at the Gospel. He writes back that he did, at the consecration, and that Nonna went to press Theo down at the bells and found him already kneeling, and that Rosie sang the Gloria a half-beat ahead of the organ the whole way through, and Merry Christmas, Lena. Under it, on his own Wall:

body.name: Becca Lindell
body.text: Merry Christmas Jack!! Praying for your Nonna’s hand!

body: He leaves the Dell on and goes up the fourteen stairs in the dark.

The back bedroom is two twins and a nightstand, with the radiator under the window and the crucifix over the door, and the alley light coming through the blind in slats. Theo has Danny’s bed, under Nonna’s cedar-chest quilt. Jack has his own. On Danny’s shelf over the beds the Browns pennant has faded to pink, and Danny at sixteen grins out of a frame in his Mooney jersey beside the JV trophy and its little gold man. The thermostat went down at eleven, the way it does; Frank calls it sleeping weather. Through the wall his father is snoring in two parts.
At two minutes past three the RAZR goes off under Jack’s pillow and puts a square of blue light on the ceiling.

body.text: merry christmas. describe the snow globe. be specific

body: In California it’s two minutes past midnight. She must have sat up waiting for it to be Christmas where she is, and then not waited one minute more. He’s grinning at the inside of his own elbow before he’s finished reading. He gets the quilt up over his head like he’s ten with a flashlight and does it with his thumbs, and T9 gives him *crucifix* on the first try, which he decides to take as a sign.

body.text: back bedroom. 2 twin beds. crucifix over the door. the little gold man on the shelf still has 1 arm
dad snoring in 2 parts thru the wall. nonna asleep in her chair downstairs. a roommate who doesnt sleep. old snow out the window and nothing falling. needs shaking

body: He laughs into the mattress with no sound, so the bed shakes. Then he lies there with the phone shut in his fist and the grin still on him, in the bed he slept in every night until August, with the house asleep under him at last and the snow gray under the alley light, and he wouldn’t trade a minute of it.

body.text: Under it in the inbox the envelope from the fish is still sitting there, unopened, where he left it.

body: He brings the quilt down off his face. The blue goes off the ceiling when the phone shuts, and the room is slats again.
From the other bed, from the dark, Theo says, “Merry Christmas, Costigan.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall.

choices.key: In Danny’s room at three on Christmas morning you told Theo that Skye had told you.
response: Nothing from the other bed. Out on the street a car goes by slow in the snow, and its lights come in through the blind and cross the ceiling and go down the wall.
“It always is,” Theo says. Then nothing.
A while later Theo says, “It isn’t six in the morning.”
Jack lies with the RAZR shut on his chest, ready for it.
“Never mind,” Theo says. “Merry Christmas.” The quilt rustles; he’s turned over toward the wall. “You answered your phone all week.”

It starts to rain not long after. Jack hears it come: a few drops on the glass behind the blind, then the whole window, then the downspout by the side door beginning to run, and under all of it the sound of the snow in the yard starting to go.
